# Femp

> Femp (also called Femp AI, by Femp AI, Inc.) is an assistant you text on WhatsApp or use in the Femp app, extended with plugins. Femp for DTC brands (in beta) runs operations for Shopify and Amazon stores: the pixel, ad spend against real sales, search and AI-assistant rankings, stock, chargebacks, the store's Gmail inbox and social posts. Femp Job Hunter and Femp Finance are coming soon. Femp acts only after the person says yes. Free during the beta.

Femp never changes prices, stock or checkout. Ads access is read-only. Product SEO and blog edits happen only after the owner says yes, and can be undone.

---

# What Femp does for your store

URL: https://femp.ai/dtc/features/

Femp is an AI operations assistant for Shopify and Amazon brands. It watches the parts of the store that slip when you're busy and tells you on WhatsApp when something needs you, with the fix ready.

● In short

 - Stock: live levels from Shopify and Amazon FBA, with days of cover for each product.

 - Ads: Meta and Google spend checked against what your store actually sold. Read-only.

 - Findability: a 0–100 score across Google, marketplaces and AI assistants such as ChatGPT and Perplexity, plus fixes you approve.

 - Inbox: chargebacks, supplier delays, account warnings and reviews flagged from your store's Gmail, with replies drafted.

 - Social (coming soon): daily stories and short videos made from your store, posted to every channel in one tap.

 - Orders and team: ask anything about sales and buyers, and add teammates who chat from their own WhatsApp.

## Stock: days of cover, not just counts

Femp reads live inventory from Shopify and Amazon FBA and works out how many days each product lasts at its current pace. You set your own alert limits. A daily stock automation lists what's out, what runs out within a week, and whether you're still paying for ads on something that's about to sell out.

Why days of cover matters: "40 left" sounds fine until you sell nine a day. Read more in Days of cover: the stock number that stops your best seller selling out.

## Ads: spend checked against real sales

Meta and Google each take credit for the same sale. Femp compares yesterday's spend in Meta Ads and Google Ads with the orders your Shopify store actually took, so ad sets that lose money show up the next morning, together with the budget change Femp would make. Femp never edits your ads; access is read-only and you make the change yourself.

Background: Are your ads making money? Check ROAS against real store sales.

## Findability: found on Google and in ChatGPT

More shoppers ask ChatGPT, Perplexity and Google's AI answers what to buy. Femp gives each store a 0–100 findability score across Google, marketplaces and AI assistants, then researches three fresh ideas on the web every afternoon. Reply with a number and Femp rewrites the product title, description, image alt text or a blog post. Every edit waits for your yes and can be undone.

The checklist behind it: How to get your products found on Google and in ChatGPT.

## Inbox: the emails that matter, flagged

Once you connect your store's Gmail, Femp checks it every hour for chargebacks, supplier delays, marketplace account warnings and reviews. It tells you which ones need you and drafts the replies for you to send. A chargeback with a deadline doesn't get buried under newsletters.

On disputes: Shopify chargebacks: how to answer every dispute before the deadline.

## Social: stories from your store, on every channel (coming soon)

Most owners run their own social and go quiet when the store gets busy. Femp will hand you two or three finished stories each morning, made from what happened in your store: a restock, a new review, a launch, a best seller, plus angles from what competitors and Amazon alternatives are posting. One tap posts a story to Instagram and Facebook, then TikTok, YouTube Shorts and Pinterest, cropped to each channel's shape. Femp tracks which stories sold and offers to boost the winners as ads. Nothing posts without your yes.

The playbook behind it: Your store makes a story every day. Here's how to post it everywhere.

## Orders: who's buying, and buying again

Ask in plain words: sales by day or week, new versus repeat buyers, best sellers, where orders came from, and what's still waiting to ship. Femp answers from your connected data and suggests a next step. It reads buyers' order history, not their names, emails or addresses.

## Automations you set up in one message

Tell Femp what to watch and when, and it becomes an automation that runs in your time zone: "every morning at 9, check stock", "tell me if my pixel misses sales", "every Monday, send me last week's profit". Start from ready-made automations or describe your own. Femp stays quiet when nothing is wrong. See how it works.

## Team and memory

Add a teammate and they chat with Femp from their own WhatsApp: the person who packs orders can ask what's still to ship. Femp remembers your preferences, so nobody has to repeat them.

# How Femp works

URL: https://femp.ai/dtc/how-it-works/

Femp lives where you already are: WhatsApp, or the Femp app. Setup takes a few minutes. Then you tell it what to automate.

## 1. Say hi on WhatsApp

Message Femp on WhatsApp. It replies with a personal link to connect your store. Femp is free during the beta.

## 2. Connect your tools through their own approval screens

Each connection uses the platform's official sign-in and consent screen: Shopify, Amazon Seller Central, Meta Ads, Google Ads, Google Search Console and Gmail. Femp never sees or keeps your passwords or one-time codes. Connect only what you want, and disconnect any of them from the app at any time. Details on the integrations page.

## 3. Get your first stock check in minutes

As soon as your store is connected, Femp runs a stock check and sends what's out, what's running low and how many days each product has left.

## 4. Set up your automations

Tell Femp what to watch and when, in your own words. Pick from ready-made automations or describe your own:

 You say | What you get | 

 "Every morning at 9, check stock" | What's out, what runs out within a week at today's pace, and whether it's still advertised | 

 "Review my ads every day before lunch" | Yesterday's Meta and Google spend against real Shopify sales, with the budget change to make | 

 "Tell me if my pixel misses sales" | A message the day Meta or Google stop counting purchases your store took | 

 "Watch my Google and ChatGPT rankings" | Where you rank, what slipped, and the pages to rewrite | 

 "Check the inbox every hour" | Chargebacks, supplier delays, account warnings and reviews from your store's Gmail, with replies drafted | 

 "Every Monday, send me last week's profit" | Sales minus ad spend, fees and refunds, by product | 

Every automation runs on your store's real data, in your time zone. Change or stop one any time by saying so. If it finds nothing worth your time, Femp doesn't message you.

## 5. Talk it through, then Femp does it

When Femp finds something, it explains it in plain words and suggests what to do, like a teammate would. Ask questions, push back or change the plan; once you give the go-ahead, it handles it and tells you when it's done. Edits can be undone, and Femp never touches your prices, stock or checkout.

## 6. Ask anything, any time

Ask Femp about the store in plain words whenever you want: "how many orders today?", "which ads lost money last week?", "what's still to ship?". Teammates you add can ask too, from their own WhatsApp.

## Shopify

Femp reads orders, products and inventory to work out days of cover, sales and repeat buyers, and to compare ad spend with real sales. With your approval it can improve product titles, descriptions and image alt text, and publish blog posts, which helps your products show up on Google and in AI assistants. See how products get found in ChatGPT.

## Amazon Seller Central

Femp reads your Amazon orders and FBA stock alongside Shopify, so days of cover reflects everything you sell, not just one channel.

## Meta Ads and Google Ads

Read-only. Femp checks each morning whether yesterday's spend turned into real store sales and suggests the budget change it would make. You make any change yourself in the ads manager.

## Google Search Console

Search data feeds the afternoon findability check: which searches find you, which pages are slipping, and what to fix first.

## Gmail

Connect the inbox your store uses and Femp checks it every hour for emails that cost money if missed: chargebacks with deadlines, supplier delays, marketplace account warnings and reviews. It drafts replies; you send them.

## Coming next

For social: Instagram and Facebook first, then TikTok, YouTube and Pinterest, so Femp can post the stories you approve. More channels and marketplaces are planned. If you need one, say so on WhatsApp or email support@femp.ai.

# Security and ground rules

URL: https://femp.ai/dtc/security/

Femp works for you, and you stay in charge. These are the rules it follows with your store and your customers' data.

## What Femp will and won't do

 - Never touches your prices, stock or checkout.

 - Never edits your ads. Meta Ads and Google Ads access is read-only.

 - Changes only what you approve. Product SEO and blog edits happen after your yes, and every edit can be undone.

 - Drafts emails, doesn't send them. You send replies from your own inbox.

## Your customers' data

 - Femp reads buyers' order history, not their names, emails or addresses.

 - Answers are worked out from your store's data for you and your team only.

## Connections and credentials

 - Every connection uses the platform's own sign-in and approval screen (Shopify, Amazon, Meta, Google).

 - Access tokens are encrypted with AES-256.

 - Femp never keeps passwords or one-time codes.

 - Disconnect any connection from the app at any time. See integrations.

## Retention and deletion

 - Chat history is deleted after 90 days.

 - Delete your account from the app in one step.

The full policy is in the privacy policy. Questions: support@femp.ai.

# 47 ops jobs you can hand to an AI assistant, and the ones you shouldn't

URL: https://femp.ai/blog/ai-operations-assistant-for-dtc-brands/

Most of what an e-commerce operations hire does is watching, reconciling, chasing and filing. That is exactly the work an always-on assistant is good at. Here is the full list, sorted by where the money is.

If you run a Shopify brand, and probably an Amazon store next to it, your day is split across eight to twelve tools: Shopify admin, Seller Central, Meta Ads Manager, Google Ads, Klaviyo, your 3PL portal, your inbox, your bank and a spreadsheet that holds it all together. Each one has a dashboard. None of them tells you what you should do this morning.

That gap is why brands hire their first operations person. We read about forty job postings for e-commerce coordinators, DTC operations managers, Amazon account managers and offshore virtual assistants to see what that person actually does. Roughly two-thirds of the listed duties are monitoring, reconciling, chasing and filing. The rest is creative work, strategy and negotiation.

The first group is what an AI operations assistant can take over. This guide lists those jobs in five groups, ordered by where the money is.

 ● In short

 - An ops assistant earns its keep on money in (ads, carts, chargebacks), money leaking (fees, overcharges, deductions) and deadlines (stock-outs, disputes, filings).

 - It should reach you where you already are (WhatsApp or text), with the fix ready, and act only after you say yes.

 - Creative, brand and campaign strategy stay with people. The assistant hands those off cleanly.

## What a day looks like

A morning message with yesterday's numbers and the three or four decisions that need you. Interruptions during the day only when money or a deadline is at stake. A weekly review on Friday. Each time you reply with a number or a "yes", and the assistant does the work, logs it and remembers your preference.

 FempWhatsApp · 9:00 am

 Morning. Lip Oil runs out Friday at 9 a day, and its ads are still spending $60 a day. Your supplier delivers in 3 days. Reorder 150?

 Also: chargeback on order #1043 ($96), reply due in 5 days. I drafted it with the tracking proof.

 reorder 150, send the reply

 Done. I'll tell you when the bank decides.

 Illustrative example of a Femp stock automation.

## 1. Growth: money on the table

These are the jobs an owner pays for because they show up in revenue.

 - Ad budget checks. Flag ad sets below your ROAS floor for several days, compared with what actually sold in the store rather than what the ad platform claims. How to check ROAS against real sales.

 - Chargebacks. Catch every dispute, gather tracking, delivery proof and customer messages, and draft the response before the deadline. Answering every dispute.

 - Abandoned-cart recovery. Most carts are abandoned (Baymard's long-running average is about 70%). The flows exist; the job is noticing when one breaks and picking high-value carts, such as repeat buyers, for a personal offer.

 - Win-back and churn. Spot lapsed repeat buyers and subscribers who skipped cycles, and draft the win-back.

 - Restock waitlists. When a sold-out item is back, tell the people who asked.

 - Carrier refunds, 3PL overcharges and retailer deductions. Money you already earned and quietly lose. Where it hides.

## 2. Operations: the day keeps running

 - Inventory and reorders. Days of cover per item against supplier lead time, a reorder suggestion, and a nudge when the ETA slips. Days of cover, explained.

 - Amazon account health. Suppressed listings, policy warnings, IP complaints and Buy Box loss, with a fix drafted inside Amazon's 72-hour Account Health Assurance window.

 - Shipping and 3PL exceptions. Orders stuck for two days, mis-picks and backorders, with the escalation drafted and customers told before they ask.

 - Refund approvals. Refunds over your limit and VIP complaints come to you with context; everything else stays in the helpdesk.

 - Supplier follow-ups. Chase ETAs, samples and quotes, and recalculate landed cost when duties change. With the US $800 de minimis exemption gone since 2025, landed cost moves more than it used to.

 - Listing and site audits. Broken links, stale promos, policy words that get listings suppressed.

## 3. Analytics: numbers you see without asking

 - Morning brief. Sales by channel, ad spend and return on it, cash and upcoming payouts, plus the decisions due today.

 - Margin by product and channel. Contribution margin after ads, shipping, fulfillment, fees and returns, so you know which products lose money.

 - Customer metrics. New versus repeat buyers, time to second order, cohort retention, with the change explained in a sentence.

 - Weekly review. Revenue, margin, average order value, repeat rate, returns by product, and what to do next week.

## 4. Housekeeping

 - App audit. Paid apps you haven't opened in 60 days.

 - Inbox triage. Separate chargebacks, supplier delays, account warnings and reviews from the noise, and draft the replies.

 - Renewals. Domain, trademark, insurance, carrier and 3PL contracts, with time to renegotiate.

 - SOPs. Write down how a task was done so a person can take it over.

## 5. Accounting and regulatory

Every item here has a date, a penalty or a lawsuit behind it, and almost none of it lives in the tools you open daily: sales tax nexus, quarterly estimates, 1099s, state annual reports, SMS consent, packaging EPR, accessibility. The assistant is not your accountant or lawyer. Its job is to know your calendar, chase the documents they need, and say plainly when a rule changed. The DTC compliance calendar.

## What should stay human

Creative, brand voice, campaign strategy, supplier negotiation and lifecycle experiments. An assistant can monitor a campaign and draft a brief, but deciding what your brand says is your job, or your agency's. A good assistant knows the difference and hands off cleanly.

## What Femp does today

Femp is our take on this. Today it covers the jobs owners ask about most:

 Job | What Femp does | 

 Stock | Reads Shopify and Amazon FBA stock, warns before items run out, estimates days of cover. | 

 Orders | Sales by day or week, what sold, new versus repeat buyers, what's still to ship. | 

 Ads | Compares Meta and Google spend with real Shopify sales and flags losing ad sets. Read-only. | 

 Search & SEO | Scores findability on Google, marketplaces and AI assistants, and rewrites titles, descriptions, alt text and blog posts after you say yes. | 

 Inbox | Reads the store's Gmail hourly for chargebacks, supplier delays, account warnings and reviews, and drafts replies. | 

 Automations | Set up any automation in one message: "every Monday, send me last week's profit". | 

The money-recovery and compliance jobs above are on our roadmap, in roughly the order the money shows up. If one of them would change your week, tell us; that is how we decide what comes next.

# Your store makes a story every day. Here's how to post it everywhere.

URL: https://femp.ai/blog/dtc-social-media-stories-from-your-store/

Most owners make their own social content, run out of time and go quiet. The fix isn't more inspiration. Your store already produces something worth posting every day: a restock, a review, a launch, a best seller. The work is turning it into a story fast and getting it onto every channel.

In Adobe Express's survey of more than 400 business owners, 7 in 10 said they felt burnt out by content creation and 68% had taken a break from posting because of it. Only 18% posted every day; 44% posted once a week. Constant Contact found that 47% of small business owners run their company's social media themselves. If you sell on Shopify or Amazon, that's probably you, fitting it in between orders and stock.

 ● In short

 - Stop starting from a blank page. Every restock, review, launch and best seller is a story.

 - Make one vertical video or frame, then cut it to each channel's shape: 9:16, 4:5 and 2:3 cover almost everything.

 - Put a tracked link on every story so you can see which ones sold, and spend ad money only on those.

## Your store is the content calendar

The posts that work for small brands are rarely clever. They're news from the store, told plainly. These happen every week whether you plan them or not:

 What happened | The story | 

 A sold-out product is back | “It's back.” Show the product, how many people asked, and how many you have. | 

 A 5-star review came in | The review on screen over the product photo, with the customer's first name if they agreed. | 

 A new product or variant | A 10-second reveal: packaging, the product in use, the price. | 

 A best seller is running low | “Last 40 of this batch.” Only when it's true, and only if you won't sell out mid-campaign. | 

 Buyers compare you with alternatives | Side by side: what you do differently, in claims you can back up. | 

 A batch was made or packed | Behind the scenes from the bench, the kitchen or the warehouse. | 

 A customer posted your product | Repost it with their permission and credit them. | 

Check stock before you post. Promoting a product you're about to run out of wastes the attention you just earned; see days of cover.

## Make it once, cut it for every channel

Shoot or build everything vertical, then crop. One 9:16 story becomes a Reel, a TikTok and a YouTube Short; a 4:5 crop goes in the feed; a 2:3 version goes to Pinterest.

 Where | Shape | Watch out for | 

 Instagram and Facebook Stories | 9:16, 1080 × 1920 | Keep text away from the top and bottom, where the app puts the profile name and reply bar. Facebook video stories stop at 60 seconds. | 

 Reels, TikTok, YouTube Shorts | 9:16, 1080 × 1920 | The first 2 seconds decide whether people keep watching. Put the product or the hook on screen at once. | 

 Instagram and Facebook feed | 4:5, 1080 × 1350 | Takes more of the screen than square. | 

 Pinterest | 2:3, 1000 × 1500 | Pins live for months: write a title someone would search for. | 

## Posting to every channel automatically

You don't have to open five apps. The platforms let approved tools post for you, with a few limits worth knowing:

 - Instagram lets tools publish Stories, Reels and feed posts, but Stories only for Business accounts, not Creator accounts. Check which one you have in the app's account settings.

 - Facebook Pages can publish photo and video stories and Reels the same way.

 - TikTok keeps posts from a tool private until TikTok has audited that tool, so ask any scheduler whether it's audited.

 - YouTube treats a short vertical upload as a Short; there's no separate upload.

 - Pinterest accepts video pins from tools, though uploads are less reliable than images.

Meta also lets you label AI-generated images and video when you post. If a scene in your story was generated rather than filmed, label it.

## Track which stories sold

Likes don't pay for stock. Give every story its own link (a UTM tag or a short code) and check Shopify a day later: sessions, orders and revenue from that story. After a few weeks you'll know which kinds of story sell for your brand, and the calendar writes itself.

When an organic story clearly beats your usual results, that's the one to put money behind. Meta lets you boost an existing post or story as an ad, so you're spending on something already proven rather than guessing. Then check the ad against real orders, not Meta's own numbers; see ROAS against real sales.

## Rules that apply to stories too

 - Customer posts: ask before reposting and credit the person. Don't edit what they said.

 - Reviews: don't show only the good ones if you're presenting them as typical, and say so if a review was incentivised. The FTC's review rule carries real penalties; see our compliance calendar.

 - Comparisons: “lasts twice as long” needs a test behind it.

 - Creators: paid or gifted posts need a clear disclosure, such as the platform's paid-partnership label.

## How Femp handles it

Social is coming to Femp. Each morning Femp will hand you two or three finished stories made from your store's own news and products, plus angles from what competitors and Amazon alternatives are posting. One tap posts a story to Instagram and Facebook first, then TikTok, YouTube and Pinterest, cropped to each channel. Femp tells you which stories sold and offers to boost the winners. Nothing posts without your yes. Join the waitlist to get it first, with $100 in free credits.

# Your Meta pixel is missing sales. Here's how to tell, and how to fix it.

URL: https://femp.ai/blog/meta-pixel-missing-purchases-shopify/

Shopify says 64 orders. Meta says 46. The missing 18 aren't a reporting quirk: Meta's algorithm learns from the purchases it sees, so a leaky pixel quietly makes every campaign worse.

Most owners notice a broken pixel the expensive way. ROAS drops, a campaign that worked last month looks like it stopped working, and the budget gets cut on ads that were selling fine. The ads didn't change. The tracking did.

 ● In short

 - Compare Shopify orders with Meta purchase events for the same day. A small steady gap is normal. A sudden drop is a break.

 - The usual causes: a theme change, old code in checkout, a consent banner, or browser-only tracking.

 - The fix that lasts: one connection through Meta's own Shopify app, with server-side tracking (Conversions API) turned on.

## Why a missing purchase costs you twice

First, reporting: Meta shows fewer sales than you made, so good ads look unprofitable and you cut them. Second, delivery: Meta decides who sees your ads based on the purchases it can see. Feed it two thirds of your buyers and it learns from two thirds of the signal. Campaigns take longer to exit the learning phase, and lookalike audiences are built from an incomplete list.

It also breaks the check that matters most: ad spend against real store sales. If the platform numbers are wrong, you need a second source of truth, and that's your Shopify orders.

## Check it in five minutes

 - In Shopify, note yesterday's online store orders. Use the same time zone as your Meta ad account.

 - In Meta Events Manager, open your pixel and look at Purchase events for the same day.

 - Compare. Some gap is normal, because some buyers block tracking or decline cookies. What you're looking for is a change: a gap that was 5% last month and is 30% this week.

 - Open the Diagnostics tab in Events Manager. Meta lists duplicate events, missing parameters and drops in event volume there.

 - Place a test order with the Meta Pixel Helper browser extension running, or use Test events in Events Manager, and confirm a Purchase arrives.

Check the other direction too. If Meta shows more purchases than Shopify, the pixel is probably installed twice, for example once by an app and once in the theme, and every sale is counted double.

## What usually breaks it

 Cause | What happens | 

 A new or edited theme | Pixel code pasted into the old theme doesn't come along. Page views and add-to-carts vanish first. | 

 Old checkout code | Shopify has been retiring checkout.liquid and the "additional scripts" box on the Thank you and Order status pages. Tracking pasted there stops firing once the store is upgraded. | 

 Consent banners | A cookie banner that blocks tracking until consent is given, misconfigured, can block it for everyone. | 

 Browser-only tracking | Ad blockers, Safari's tracking limits and iOS settings stop browser pixels from reporting. Server-side events still get through. | 

 Duplicate installs | An app and the theme both send Purchase, without a shared event ID, so Meta counts every order twice. | 

## The fix that lasts

 - Use one connection. Install Meta's Facebook & Instagram app in Shopify and connect your pixel there. Remove pixel code pasted into the theme and any older tracking apps.

 - Turn on server-side tracking. In the app's data-sharing settings, choose the highest level. That sends purchases from Shopify's servers through the Conversions API as well as from the browser, and Meta removes the duplicates.

 - Move custom tracking to Customer events. Anything else you track at checkout belongs in Shopify's Settings → Customer events as a custom pixel, not in the theme.

 - Check Event Match Quality. Events Manager scores how well your events match Meta accounts. Sending email and phone (hashed, which the app does for you) raises it.

 - Do the same for Google. Connect through the Google & YouTube app and turn on enhanced conversions.

Then repeat the five-minute check after every theme change, checkout change or new app. That's when tracking breaks.

## How Femp handles it

 ugh. what do I do?

# Your ads say they're profitable. Your store disagrees.

URL: https://femp.ai/blog/ads-roas-against-real-sales/

Meta says 3.4×. Google says 2.9×. Add up the sales they both claim and you sold more than your store took in. Here's a simple daily check that keeps ad spend honest.

For most DTC brands, ads are the largest variable cost after the products themselves. They're also the cost most likely to be overstated by the tool reporting it. Meta and Google each attribute sales to their own ads with their own windows and models, so the same order can show up in both reports. Neither knows what your store actually took in.

You don't need a full attribution platform to catch the expensive mistakes. You need a daily check of spend against real sales, and a rule for what to do when it looks wrong.

 ● In short

 - Track blended ROAS (store revenue ÷ total ad spend) or MER every day. It can't double count.

 - For each ad set or campaign, compare spend with the sales of the products it promotes.

 - Set a floor (for example ROAS under 1.0 for three days) and a rule: cut, pause or move budget.

## Platform ROAS versus blended ROAS

Platform ROAS is what Ads Manager shows: revenue the platform attributes to its ads, divided by spend. Useful for comparing ads on the same platform, unreliable as a total.

Blended ROAS, sometimes called MER (marketing efficiency ratio), is all store revenue for the day divided by all ad spend. It's crude, but it's real money on both sides of the line.

blended ROAS = store revenue ÷ (Meta + Google + other ad spend)

Watch the trend. If spend rises 30% and blended ROAS falls from 3.1 to 2.2, the extra spend isn't buying much, whatever each platform says.

## Find the ad sets losing money

Blended numbers hide the culprit. To find it, line up each campaign or ad set with the products it promotes and their sales in Shopify:

 Ad set | Spend yesterday | Product sales | Ratio | 

 Lip Oil prospecting | $60 | $192 | 3.2× | 

 Clay Mask prospecting | $45 | $27 | 0.6× | 

 Retargeting | $30 | $57 | 1.9× | 

This isn't perfect attribution, and it doesn't need to be. Clay Mask spent $45 to sell $27 of product. Even with generous assumptions, that ad set is losing money.

## Know your break-even ROAS

A ratio of 1.0 means you got your ad spend back in revenue, not profit. To break even on a sale you also need to cover the product, shipping, payment fees and returns:

break-even ROAS = 1 ÷ contribution margin before ads

If a product keeps 50% of its price after goods, shipping and fees, you need 2.0× just to break even on the first order. Repeat purchases can justify going lower for new customers, but decide that on purpose.

## A daily rule that stops slow leaks

 - Every morning, check yesterday's spend by campaign against product sales.

 - Flag anything under break-even for three days in a row. One bad day is noise.

 - Check stock before you scale a winner. Doubling the budget on an item with four days of cover just buys a stock-out (see days of cover).

 - Look for broken basics: a disapproved ad, a pixel that stopped firing, a landing page that's out of stock.

 - Decide: cut, pause, or move the budget to what's working.

## How Femp handles it

Set up an ads automation ("review my ads every morning") and Femp compares yesterday's Meta and Google spend with what actually sold in your Shopify store, and tells you which ad sets are losing money with the change it would make. Femp's ads access is read-only: it never edits your campaigns. You make the change in Ads Manager, and it checks again the next day.

 ok, cutting it now

 Thanks. I'll check it again tomorrow.

# 7 out of 10 carts never check out. Here's how to win some back.

URL: https://femp.ai/blog/shopify-abandoned-carts-recover-sales/

Most people who add to cart never pay. Some were only browsing. Plenty left over something you can fix: a surprise shipping cost, a forced account, a checkout that asked too much.

Baymard Institute's running average of published studies puts online cart abandonment at about 70%. You won't get that to zero, and you shouldn't try: many carts are window shopping. But the buyers who reached checkout and stopped are the warmest people your store will ever see, and you already paid to bring them there.

 ● In short

 - Fix the reasons first. Surprise costs at checkout are the top reason buyers leave.

 - Then recover: a reminder within an hour, a second the next day, and a discount only at the end, if at all.

 - Watch which products get abandoned most. A pattern there is a price or shipping problem.

## Abandoned cart or abandoned checkout?

They're different in Shopify. A cart is anyone who added a product. A checkout is someone who started paying and typed an email or phone number. Shopify can only follow up on the second kind, and lists them under Orders → Abandoned checkouts. Reaching people who left from the cart page needs a logged-in customer or a marketing app that captures their email earlier.

## Why buyers leave

Baymard's surveys of shoppers who abandoned a checkout keep finding the same reasons near the top:

 - Extra costs. Shipping, taxes or fees that appear only at checkout. This is the top reason by a wide margin.

 - Being asked to create an account.

 - Delivery too slow, or no delivery date shown.

 - Not trusting the site with card details.

 - A long or confusing checkout.

 - An unclear returns policy.

## Fix the checkout first

 - Show shipping early. Put the cost, or the free-shipping threshold, on the product page and in the cart.

 - Allow guest checkout. In Shopify's customer account settings, keep accounts optional.

 - Turn on express payments. Shop Pay, Apple Pay, Google Pay and PayPal skip most of the form.

 - Show a delivery estimate on the product page, not only at the end.

 - Put the returns policy and reviews near the Add to cart button.

## A recovery sequence that doesn't nag

 When | What to send | 

 Within 1 hour | A plain reminder with the product photo and a link back to their checkout. No discount. | 

 About 24 hours | Answer the likely objection: delivery time, returns, reviews from other buyers. | 

 48–72 hours | Optional: a small incentive, ideally only for first-time buyers, so regulars don't learn to wait for a code. | 

Shopify's Marketing → Automations has an abandoned checkout flow you can edit. Only send SMS to people who agreed to texts at checkout; see the SMS consent rules in our compliance calendar.

## Measure it weekly

 - Recovery rate: recovered orders divided by abandoned checkouts that left an email or phone.

 - Abandoned by product: one product abandoned far more than others usually means its shipping cost or price looks wrong at checkout.

 - Abandoned by step: buyers leaving at shipping point to cost. Leaving at payment points to trust or payment options.

## How Femp handles it

Abandoned-cart reports are coming to Femp: a daily look at which products and checkout steps lose buyers, with the recovery message ready for you to send. Join the waitlist to get it first, with $100 in free credits.

# Most chargebacks are lost to a buried email. Here's how to win them.

URL: https://femp.ai/blog/shopify-chargebacks-answer-every-dispute/

A chargeback you don't answer is a chargeback you lose: the order, the product and a fee. Most small brands lose them not because the case was weak, but because the email got buried.

When a customer disputes a charge with their bank, the money is taken back from your payout right away, and you're charged a dispute fee (on Shopify Payments in the US it's $15). You then have a fixed window to respond with evidence. Miss it and the dispute is decided against you automatically.

Industry estimates put the average merchant win rate around 30%, and lower for manual, rushed responses. Plenty of disputes are winnable: the package was delivered, the customer used the product, or they forgot they bought it. What loses them is time.

 ● In short

 - Answer every dispute. Unanswered ones are automatic losses.

 - Match your evidence to the reason code: delivery proof for "not received", product page and policy for "not as described".

 - Watch your dispute ratio. Visa and Mastercard monitoring programs start at roughly 1% of transactions, and fines follow.

## Where disputes show up

In Shopify admin under Orders → Chargebacks, and by email to the store owner. The email is the problem: it lands next to supplier invoices, app notifications and customer messages, and the deadline is in the body, not the subject line. Put every new dispute on a list with its due date the day it arrives.

## Evidence that wins, by reason

 Reason | What to include | 

 Product not received | Tracking showing delivery to the shipping address, delivery date, signature or photo if you have it, matching billing and shipping details. | 

 Not as described | Screenshot of the product page at time of purchase, your return policy, and any messages where you offered a return or replacement. | 

 Fraudulent / unauthorized | AVS and CVV match, IP location, the customer's order history with you, account login, and any emails they sent after ordering. | 

 Subscription canceled | Sign-up terms they agreed to, renewal reminders sent, and proof no cancellation request came in before the charge. | 

 Duplicate / incorrect amount | Both orders showing different items or dates, or the receipt matching the amount charged. | 

Write a short, factual cover note: what was ordered, when it was delivered, what the customer said afterwards. The person reviewing it at the bank has a few minutes per case.

## Prevent the next one

 - Use a recognizable descriptor on card statements, so customers don't dispute a charge they don't recognize.

 - Answer "where is my order?" fast. Many "not received" disputes start as an unanswered support email.

 - Add signature confirmation on high-value orders.

 - Review risky orders before shipping: mismatched billing and shipping, or customers who've disputed before.

 - Offer an easy refund. A refund costs less than a lost dispute plus the fee.

## Keep an eye on the ratio

Card networks track disputes as a share of your transactions. Cross their thresholds and you enter a monitoring program with fines, and your payment provider may hold funds or close the account. A small brand with a bad month can get close quickly. Check your rate monthly.

## How Femp handles it

Femp reads your store's Gmail every hour. When a dispute arrives, it messages you with the order, the amount and the due date, pulls the tracking and order history, and drafts the response for you to review and send.

 FempWhatsApp · 2:14 pm

 Chargeback on order #1043 ($96), reason "not received". The reply is due in 5 days. UPS shows it delivered to the shipping address on the 3rd. I drafted the response with the tracking proof. Want to see it?

 send me the draft

# Why ChatGPT doesn't recommend your products, and how to fix it

URL: https://femp.ai/blog/products-found-google-chatgpt/

Shoppers used to type "rose serum" into Google. Now many of them ask an AI assistant "what's a good rose serum for dry skin under $50?" If your product isn't in the answer, it isn't on the shelf.

Search is splitting in two. Classic Google results still send most of the traffic, but a growing share of product research starts in AI assistants: ChatGPT shows product cards with prices and links, Perplexity has shopping answers, and Google puts AI Overviews above the blue links. They all pull from the same places: your product pages, your structured data, merchant feeds, and what other sites say about you.

The good news for small brands: these answers reward clear, specific information more than a big ad budget. A well-described product from a small store can be the best answer to a narrow question.

 ● In short

 - Write titles and descriptions that answer who it's for, what it does and how it differs, using the words shoppers use.

 - Give machines clean data: Product structured data, a Google Merchant Center feed, GTINs, price and availability.

 - Get mentioned elsewhere: reviews, comparison articles and "best of" lists are where AI answers find you.

## Test where you stand

Pick five questions a customer would actually ask, specific ones like "best fragrance-free lip oil for sensitive skin" rather than your brand name. Then check:

 - Google: do you appear on the first page, in Shopping results or in the AI Overview?

 - ChatGPT and Perplexity: does the answer mention your brand or link to your product?

 - Amazon and other marketplaces: where do you rank for the same words?

Write the results down. Re-run the same questions monthly. It's the simplest findability score there is.

## Product titles that match questions

"Aurora" tells a shopper and a model nothing. "Aurora Rose Face Serum for Dry Skin, 30 ml, Fragrance-Free" answers four questions at once. Lead with what the product is, then the attribute people filter on (skin type, size, material, use). Keep the brand voice in the description, not the title.

## Descriptions that answer, not just sell

 - Open with one plain sentence: what it is and who it's for.

 - List the facts a comparison needs: ingredients or materials, size, how to use, what it's not suited for.

 - Add a short FAQ with real customer questions from your inbox and reviews.

 - Write image alt text that describes the product, not "IMG_2041".

## Give machines clean data

 - Product structured data. Most Shopify themes output it; check with Google's Rich Results Test that price, availability, brand and reviews are present.

 - Google Merchant Center. Connect it through the Google & YouTube app on Shopify to appear in free Shopping listings. Fix disapprovals promptly.

 - GTINs and consistent names across Shopify, Amazon and your feed, so systems can tell it's the same product.

 - Don't block crawlers you want. If your robots.txt or a security tool blocks OAI-SearchBot, PerplexityBot or Googlebot, those engines can't read your pages.

## Be talked about

AI answers lean heavily on third-party sources: review sites, Reddit threads, gift guides and comparison articles. A few honest mentions on sites that already rank for your category do more than a dozen posts on your own blog. Send product to writers who cover your niche, and reply to reviews so there's a visible record.

## Publish content that answers buying questions

A blog post that answers "how to choose a face serum for dry skin" with a clear recommendation is the kind of page that gets cited. Write for the question, not for a keyword count, and link to the products that answer it.

## How Femp handles it

With a search automation, Femp gives your store a findability score from 0 to 100 across Google, marketplaces and AI assistants, plus three fresh ideas researched on the web. Reply with a number and it does the work: rewrites product titles, descriptions and image alt text, or drafts a blog post. Nothing changes until you say yes, and every edit can be undone.

 Illustrative example.

# Your best seller is about to sell out. This number warns you first.

URL: https://femp.ai/blog/days-of-cover-inventory/

"40 left" sounds fine until you notice you sell nine a day and your supplier needs three days. The number that matters is how many days your stock lasts.

Stock-outs rarely happen because nobody looked at inventory. They happen because somebody looked at a count, saw a reasonable-sounding number, and moved on. Forty units of your best seller feels like plenty. At nine a day it's four days, and if your supplier needs three days plus a weekend, you've already missed the window.

A stock-out costs more than the lost sales. Your ads keep spending on a product nobody can buy, and on Amazon a stock-out can cost you ranking that takes weeks to win back.

 ● In short

 - Days of cover = units available ÷ average daily sales.

 - Reorder when days of cover falls below supplier lead time + shipping + a safety buffer.

 - Count Shopify and Amazon FBA together if they draw on the same supply, and pause ads on items about to run out.

## How to calculate days of cover

Take the units you can sell now (on hand, minus anything reserved for open orders) and divide by how many you sell per day.

days of cover = available units ÷ units sold per day

For "units sold per day", use a recent window, usually the last 14 or 28 days, so a spike from one viral post doesn't distort it. If you're running a promotion, use the promotion's pace, not last month's.

 Product | Available | Sold per day | Days of cover | 

 Lip Oil | 40 | 9 | 4.4 | 

 Rose Serum | 120 | 5 | 24 | 

 Clay Mask | 210 | 6 | 35 | 

Sorted by units, Clay Mask looks like the risk and Lip Oil looks fine. Sorted by days, it's the other way round.

## Set a reorder point from lead time

Days of cover becomes useful when you compare it with how long a restock takes:

reorder when days of cover < supplier lead time + transit + safety days

 - Lead time is from PO to goods leaving the supplier. Use what actually happened last time, not the quote.

 - Transit includes receiving at your warehouse or 3PL. For Amazon, add FBA check-in time, which can stretch in Q4.

 - Safety days cover a slow supplier or a sales spike. A week is common for a steady seller; more for anything imported.

With a 21-day lead time and 11 days of cover, you're already ten days late. That is the alert worth getting: a date and an action, not a count.

## Shopify and Amazon together

If you sell on both, look at each channel's stock and its own pace. FBA stock can't fill a Shopify order unless you use Multi-Channel Fulfillment, and your 3PL stock can't fill an Amazon Prime order. A product can be fine on Shopify and two days from running out on Amazon. Count inbound shipments separately: units on a truck aren't available until they're checked in.

## Stop advertising what you can't sell

The quietest stock-out cost is ad spend. When an item hits zero, or gets close enough that you'll sell out before the restock lands, its ads keep running. Check ad spend for any product under a week of cover and decide whether to pause, cut the budget or move it to an item with plenty of stock.

## Checklist

 - Calculate days of cover per item, per channel, every morning.

 - Keep each supplier's real lead time next to it.

 - Alert when cover drops below lead time + transit + safety days.

 - Draft the PO at that point, and chase the ETA.

 - Check ad spend on anything under a week of cover.

## How Femp handles it

Femp reads live stock from Shopify and Amazon FBA and works out days of cover at the current pace. With a daily stock automation, it tells you what's out, what runs out within a week, and whether you're still advertising it. You can set your own limits ("warn me under 10 days for the serum") and ask any time: "what's running low?"

 FempWhatsApp · 9:00 am

# You're owed money in your invoices. Here's where it's hiding.

URL: https://femp.ai/blog/money-hiding-in-your-invoices/

You already earned this money. It leaks out a few dollars at a time through net payouts, carrier surcharges, 3PL invoices and retailer deductions that nobody has time to check.

Brands spend a lot of effort winning revenue and very little checking that they keep it. The leaks are small per line: a $12 surcharge, a misapplied fee, one pallet billed that isn't there. Added up over a year, they're often a few percent of revenue, and nobody at a small brand has the job of finding them.

 ● In short

 - Payouts: match each Shopify payout and Amazon settlement to orders, fees and refunds.

 - Carriers: claim late-delivery refunds and dispute wrong surcharges. Audit firms report recoverable errors of 1–5% of parcel spend.

 - 3PLs: check storage, picks and fees against your rate card. Storage is the line most often inflated.

 - Retailers: if you sell to Walmart, Target or Amazon Vendor Central, dispute invalid deductions inside the window.

## 1. Payouts that don't add up

Shopify and Amazon pay you net: sales minus fees, refunds, chargebacks, reserves and adjustments. The deposit looks plausible, so nobody checks it. Once a week, take each payout and confirm the orders, fees and refunds in it add up to the amount received. On Amazon, look for fees you can't tie to an order, such as FBA removal or disposal fees, storage charges and inventory adjustments, and for lost or damaged FBA units that haven't been reimbursed.

## 2. Carrier invoices

UPS and FedEx invoices are long and full of accessorial charges. The common recoverable items:

 - Late deliveries on guaranteed services, where the carrier's money-back guarantee applies (check your contract; some suspend it).

 - Address-correction fees on addresses that weren't wrong.

 - Dimensional weight billed on dimensions larger than your box.

 - Duplicate charges and surcharges your contract waives.

Also watch your shipping cost per order week to week. In 2026 carrier list rates rose about 5.9%, but surcharges rose faster, so the real increase for many DTC shippers was higher. If the residential surcharge share is climbing, it may be time to renegotiate or change services.

## 3. 3PL invoices

A 3PL bill mixes storage, receiving, picks, packaging and special projects. Compare it with your rate card and the 3PL's own warehouse data:

 - Storage: pallets or bins billed versus actually occupied.

 - Picks: pick fees versus orders shipped.

 - Returns and receiving: charges for work that didn't happen, or fees not in your contract.

Audit firms report that first audits commonly find errors, with storage the most inflated line. Even if your 3PL is honest, a manual billing process makes mistakes.

## 4. Retailer deductions

If you sell wholesale to big-box retailers, they deduct for shortages, late shipments, labeling and compliance issues, often automatically. Industry estimates say deductions take 2–5% of gross revenue for suppliers, and a large share are invalid. Match each deduction to the bill of lading and ship notice, and dispute inside the window; the proof that wins a shortage claim is usually a signed BOL.

## A weekly money check

 - Match last week's payouts and settlements.

 - Scan carrier invoices for late deliveries and surcharges; file claims.

 - Compare the 3PL invoice with your rate card and order count.

 - List new retailer deductions and their dispute deadlines.

 - Chase wholesale invoices past due.

 ● Where Femp is today
 Femp already reads your store's Gmail every hour and flags chargebacks, supplier delays and account warnings. Payout matching, carrier and 3PL invoice checks, and retailer deductions are on our roadmap. If recovering this money matters to you, tell us which one first.

# The DTC compliance calendar: every deadline that can cost you money

URL: https://femp.ai/blog/dtc-compliance-calendar/

Almost none of these deadlines live in the tools you open every day. Each one has a date, a penalty or a lawsuit behind it. Here they are on one page.

● Not legal or tax advice
 This is a checklist of what to ask your accountant and lawyer about, written for US brands. Thresholds and dates change; confirm the ones that apply to your business with them.

A $2M brand has more filing obligations than most owners realize: federal and state taxes, state entity reports, contractor forms, and product, marketing and privacy rules that depend on what you sell and where. Your accountant knows the tax dates. Usually nobody owns the rest.

## Sales tax: nexus and filing

 - Economic nexus. Since the 2018 Wayfair decision, states can require you to collect once your sales into them cross a threshold. Most states use $100,000 a year (some add a transaction count); California and Texas use $500,000, and New York uses $500,000 plus 100 transactions. In some states, marketplace sales count toward the threshold even though Amazon collects the tax.

 - Register before you collect. Collecting sales tax without a permit is a problem of its own.

 - Who remits. Amazon collects and remits as a marketplace facilitator. Shopify calculates tax but does not file or remit it for you.

 - Zero returns. Once registered, file on the schedule the state assigns, even when you owe nothing.

## Federal tax dates

 - Estimated taxes: April 15, June 15, September 15 and January 15. Set cash aside each month.

 - S-corp and partnership returns (1120-S, 1065): mid-March for calendar-year businesses. Late filing penalties are charged per owner, per month.

 - Payroll deposits and Form 941 quarterly. Missed payroll taxes can be assessed against owners personally.

## 1099s and W-9s

Collect a W-9 from every contractor and agency before you pay them. The 1099-NEC reporting threshold rises from $600 to $2,000 for payments made in 2026, and the federal 1099-K threshold is back to $20,000 and 200 transactions. A platform 1099-K reports gross volume, including shipping, tax and refunded orders, so it will be higher than your revenue; reconcile it before your accountant asks.

## State entity compliance

Every state where your company is registered (home state and any foreign qualifications) has an annual or biennial report and often a franchise tax. Delaware LLCs pay their annual tax by June 1. Miss these and you can lose good standing, which can block bank accounts, contracts and lawsuits.

## Marketing rules

 - SMS (TCPA). Damages run $500 to $1,500 per message. Since April 2025 the FCC requires honoring opt-outs made by "any reasonable means" within 10 business days, not just a reply of STOP. Check that your SMS tool actually honored last month's opt-outs.

 - Reviews. The FTC's rule on fake reviews and testimonials (in force since October 2024) bans buying reviews, suppressing negative ones and undisclosed insider reviews, with civil penalties per violation.

 - "Made in USA" and influencer disclosures are FTC territory too. Check claims before a campaign goes live.

 - Subscriptions. The FTC's click-to-cancel rule was struck down in 2025, but ROSCA enforcement and state auto-renewal laws (California's is among the strictest) still apply.

## Website and privacy

 - Accessibility. E-commerce sites, including many Shopify stores, receive a large share of ADA website lawsuits. Overlay widgets don't prevent them. Test theme and popup changes with a keyboard and a screen reader.

 - State privacy laws. About 20 states now have one, with different thresholds; several require honoring browser opt-out signals (Global Privacy Control). Keep your privacy policy and consent banner current.

 - Payments. Shopify's hosted checkout keeps most stores in the simplest PCI category; custom scripts on payment pages can change that.

## Product compliance

 - California Prop 65: if a warning applies, it must be shown online before purchase.

 - Cosmetics (MoCRA): facility registration and product listing with the FDA, plus adverse-event records.

 - Food and supplements: FDA food facility registrations renew between October 1 and December 31 of every even-numbered year, including 2026.

 - Children's products: a Children's Product Certificate from a CPSC-accepted lab. Amazon suspends listings without one.

 - Packaging EPR: Oregon, Colorado, California, Maine, Minnesota, Maryland and Washington have packaging laws that can make you a "producer" with registration, reporting and fees.

## Marketplace identity and trademarks

Under the INFORM Consumers Act, marketplaces must suspend high-volume sellers who don't verify their information within 10 days of a request. And keep your trademark alive: a USPTO Section 8 declaration is due between years five and six after registration, or Amazon Brand Registry can lapse with it.

## Rules that no longer apply

Stale advice is a cost too. Beneficial ownership (BOI) reporting no longer applies to US-formed companies after FinCEN's 2025 change, yet many pages still warn about it. Ask your accountant to confirm which rules apply to you before you pay someone to file something you don't need.

 ● Where Femp is today
 Femp can already run any reminder you give it on a schedule ("on the 18th, remind me about the Texas return") and flags account and policy warnings that land in your store's inbox. A full compliance calendar built from your entity, states, products and channels is on our roadmap. It will keep the calendar and chase documents, while filing stays with your accountant and lawyer.
